text: A boy looked after many sheep. (Literally: "white-haired animals.") He was bored. (Literally: "he felt there was nothing fun.") He shouted: "Wolf! Help!" (Literally: "the big bad animal has come!") Many people came running, but there was no wolf. The boy laughed: "It wasn't true!" Later he did it again. People came again, and again there was no wolf. People got angry. (Literally: "there was fire in their hearts.") Then one day, a real wolf came! The boy shouted: "Wolf! This time it's true!" But people thought he was lying again (literally: "not saying true things"), and nobody came. The wolf ate many of the sheep. If you don't tell the truth, people stop listening to you.

sketch.idea: a boy looked after many sheep (white-haired animals)
the boy was bored: he felt nothing was fun
he shouted: the big bad animal (wolf) has come, help!
the boy laughed and said: it was not true
later he shouted the same thing again
people got angry (fire in their hearts)
one day a real wolf came
the boy shouted: the wolf has come, this time it is true
sketch.why: The reader got the shout, but read 'this time it is true' as the narrator's comment, not as part of what the boy shouted. The summary says he just 'shouts the same thing', so his plea that it is true now is lost.

sketch.idea: people thought he was lying again (not saying true things)
the wolf ate many of the sheep
if you do not tell the truth, people stop listening to you

blind.whole: A boy looks after many white-haired animals (probably sheep) and is bored. For fun he shouts that a big bad animal is coming and calls for help. People hurry over, find nothing, and he laughs and says it wasn't true. He does it again, the people come again, and they get angry. Then one day a big bad animal really comes. He shouts the same thing, but the people think he is lying again, so nobody comes, and the animal eats many of his white-haired animals. The lesson: if you don't tell the truth, people stop listening to you.
blind.unsure: Sentence 2: I read kàn-hǎo as 'look after, watch over'. The gloss says 'look at - good', and it could also be read as 'thinks well of' the animals, but in this story 'looks after' fits better. 'White-haired animals' is most likely sheep, but the text only says animals with white hair or fur, so they could be some other animal. 'Big bad animal' (dà huài dòng-wù) is never named: it is some large dangerous beast that eats the white-haired animals, perhaps a wolf, but the text doesn't say which. Sentence 1: xiǎo nán-rén is literally 'little man'. I took it as a boy, though it could mean a small grown man. Sentence 8: zhè bù shì zhēn-de could mean 'this isn't real' (there was no animal) or 'I wasn't being truthful'. Both readings say the same thing here. Sentence 12: 'fire in the heart' I read as anger, not as a literal fire.

notes: Translated by hand following the translate skill, whole dictionary, no lesson. Heads-up for the test: kb_memory returns this story's own book lines (lesson none, the stories appendix) at up to 100% shared, so step 2 handed over most of the text; each reused line is named in its source and was still checked; five were changed because they did not read as meant ((1) to (5) below), and a few more for meaning or length. Changed from the book's lines: (1) "Tā jué-de méi-yǒu shénme hǎo wánr-de." has over 500 readings and none of the first 500 has jué-dé taking the thought (they end as a noun: the thing that ...), so shénme dōu bù hǎo-wánr; (2) "Hěn duō rén kuài lái le, dàn-shì méi-yǒu dà huài dòng-wù." has no reading in its first 500 with both halves as meant, so it is split, and "Dàn-shì méi-yǒu dà huài dòng-wù." alone breaks dà huài dòng-wù apart in every reading, so nà-lǐ (there) is added; (3) "Hòu-lái, …" reads only as calling out to someone (calling-hail, 2 of 2 readings), so yǐ-hòu, which has a time reading; (4) "Dà huài dòng-wù chī le hěn duō bái-sè máo-de dòng-wù.": in its first 500 readings the big bad animal is never the one who eats (all read as one long noun), so bǎ … chī le; (5) "Xiǎo nán-rén xiào le: …" reads only as two sentences side by side, so "xiào le, shuō: …"; (6) kàn became kàn-hǎo (look after); (7) the two-sentence shouts are split so each item is one sentence; also yǒu yī tiān (one day) for yǒu yī-cì (once), le added to xīn-lǐ yǒu huǒ for got angry, and tā for the boy where nothing else could be meant. Six sentences stay over 10 words (warnings only): 2, 4, 13, 14, 16, 18. A pitfall to know: jué-dé taking a thought shows in the brackets as "jué dé" (two words, the feel-state rule); "jué-dé" with a hyphen is the word used as a plain verb. Not said, by choice: "running" is weaker (kuài lái le, came quickly; pǎo is not a word, run is kuài zǒu). Worth the author's attention: kb_gloss gives nán-rén as "difficult-human being" (nán is 难 in the dictionary, so the hanzi line shows 难-人 where the book prints 男人); a blind reader may stumble on the boy. Cast: the sheep and the wolf both have dòng-wù as their head, so a short name (zhè-ge dòng-wù) would mix them up; both descriptions are 6 words or fewer and are repeated in full. Glossary proposal: wolf -> dà huài dòng-wù: the stories' own short name (this story and Little Red Riding Hood), against the 10-word form. Glossary proposal: sheep -> bái-sè máo-de dòng-wù: 6 words against the 11-word form of 羊. Glossary proposal: tell lies -> bù shuō zhēn-de: there is no entry for lie (to say false things). Glossary proposal: nobody -> méi-yǒu rén and the verb: no entry, the grammar says it and parses cleanly. Glossary proposal: one day -> Yǒu yī tiān, …: the opener for a story event. Glossary proposal: later -> Yǐ-hòu, …: Hòu-lái with a comma reads only as calling out. Glossary proposal: boy -> xiǎo nán-rén: the stories' own word; nán-hái-zi, the gloss-tier form, glosses as "difficult-still-(noun ending)" in kb_gloss. Translated before kb_memory hid the stories' own lines (HAOSHUODE_MEMORY_SKIP), so some sentences reuse the book's lines and the book overlap is higher than a fresh run would give.
